title: 1972 B-52C Lake Michigan crash
summary: A USAF B-52C Stratofortress (call sign Hiram 16) operating a low-level training flight over northern Lake Michigan crashed on January 7, 1971. The aircraft was flying at 300 to 500 ft above the water in broken to overcast skies at 2500 ft with visibility 2 miles with light snow and rime icing. After successfully scoring bomb runs on targets Echo, Foxtrot and Delta, at 6:33 pm the aircraft suddenly disappeared from radar during the bombing run on target Charlie. All nine crew members aboard were lost. No remains of the crewmen were recovered. The aircraft was 15 years old and none of the remaining B-52Cs had been modified to cope with the structural stress demands of low-level flight.

title: 1971 January 22 Surgut Aeroflot Antonov An-12 crash
summary: An Aeroflot Antonov An-12B departed Omsk Tsentralny Airport on 22 January 1971 bound for Surgut, carrying two flight crews, an engineer, loadmaster, and cargo. Upon descent toward Surgut, severe icing conditions were encountered at 400 to 1300 meters altitude. The aircraft's ice protection system was ineffective because engine bleed air valves were closed during the flight. As the aircraft descended to 1200 meters, ice accumulated on the wings, causing flow separation and a sudden loss of control. The aircraft entered an uncontrolled roll and crashed 15 kilometers short of the Surgut runway.

title: Aviogenex 130
summary: Aviogenex Flight 130, an international charter from Gatwick to Rijeka, took off at 16:33 GMT and suffered structural failure during landing on 23 May 1971. The Tupolev Tu-134A flipped over and caught fire. Investigation found that the crew might have suffered an optical illusion due to heavy showers and dusk that could have led them to believe the runway was closer and lower than it actually was. The crew executed an overly steep and fast descent in the last phase of final approach, causing a hard touchdown and breakage of the right wing, killing 78 out of 83 people.
probable_cause: Optical illusion caused by dusk, rain and water on runway led the crew to believe they were closer and higher from the runway than actually the case. The crew made a sharp nose-down input and reduced power to idle in the final phase, causing the aircraft to reach excessive speed and contact the runway with forces that broke the right wing.

The aircraft contacted the runway at speed of 260 km/h with excessive forces (vertical load of 4g and horizontal load 1.5g) on the right landing gear that broke the right wing.

summary: Hughes Airwest Flight 706, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9-31 flying from Los Angeles to Seattle with several intermediate stops, collided in midair with a U.S. Marine Corps F-4B Phantom II over the San Gabriel Mountains near Duarte, California, on 6 June 1971. The Phantom, returning to MCAS El Toro after diagnostic tests following an earlier radio failure, struck the DC-9; witnesses reported its right wing hit the center of the fuselage and its vertical stabilizer sliced through the cockpit. The NTSB calculated the two aircraft's closing rate at about 1000 ft/s and found that ten additional feet of clearance would have averted the collision.

title: Malév 110
summary: Malév Flight 110, a Tupolev Tu-134, was delayed over an hour due to poor weather before departing Budapest for Kyiv-Boryspil on September 16, 1971. Flying into heavy fog with visibility of only 1,800 meters, the crew was unable to land on the first attempt but chose to continue circling. A false generator failure indication caused the crew to switch to battery power without rectifying the signal or implementing proper power conservation. With visibility degraded to 700 meters, battery power depleting, and incorrect information from ground control, the crew deviated from the advised flight path and lost radio and radar contact. The aircraft descended too low, the right wing struck terrain at approximately 550 knots, and the Tu-134 broke apart, killing all 49 aboard.

The aircraft was climbing through 19,000 feet when the crew suddenly transmitted we are going down and mayday multiple times, stating the aircraft was out of control with no rudder control. title: Aeroflot 63
summary: Scheduled Antonov An-24 flight on 12 November 1971 from Kiev-Zhulhyany Airport to Vinnitsa Airport. summary: Aeroflot Flight 2174, an Antonov An-24B, crashed on approach to Saratov Tsentralny Airport on 1 December 1971, resulting in the death of all 57 people aboard. The aircraft encountered icing conditions during descent. As ice accumulated, the crew added power to counter effects but control was lost and the aircraft crashed at high rate of descent 13 kilometers northwest of the runway with landing gear and flaps retracted.

The anti-ice system was not activated during the descent, a reason which could not be determined.

summary: A Lockheed L-188A Electra turboprop operating a domestic passenger flight was struck by lightning on its right wing while cruising at 21,000 feet in a severe thunderstorm. A fire broke out and the aircraft suffered catastrophic structural failure with the right wing and part of the left wing separating in flight.
